582.title: The pledge under the tree
582.hook: Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged under the tree (48:18)
582.howItsDone: Many Muslims honor the Companions who pledged at Hudaybiyyah as the people of the tree, and the bay'ah, a pledge given by hand, remains a form of commitment in many communities and Sufi orders.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sakinah, the stillness sent down into anxious hearts. Your line was tranquillity comes down.

Rewind a few days before the treaty. The Prophet ﷺ has sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan into Mecca as his envoy, to explain that the Muslims have come only as pilgrims. 'Uthman doesn't come back. Hours pass, then days. A rumor runs through the camp: 'Uthman has been killed. A camp of pilgrims, far from home, armed only for travel, gathered by a tree. And the Prophet asks each of them for a pledge.

Verse eighteen of Surah Al-Fath, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah was well pleased with the believers when they swore allegiance unto thee beneath the tree." He knew what was in their hearts, the verse goes on, sent down peace of reassurance on them, and rewarded them with a near victory. The pledge is called Bay'at ar-Ridwan, the Pledge of Good Pleasure, after the word in the verse: Allah was pleased. Bay'ah is a pledge sealed with the hand, from the root of buying and selling, a deal struck palm to palm. One by one they placed their hand in his. The hadith reports say they pledged to stand firm and not to flee. Then a detail the hadith keeps. 'Uthman wasn't there to pledge. So the Prophet held up his own right hand, said this is the hand of 'Uthman, and struck it on his left, pledging on his absent friend's behalf. 'Uthman, it turned out, was alive; he'd been held in Mecca. And the tree? A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says that the next year, some who had been there couldn't find it again. Later reports, outside Bukhari, say 'Umar had a tree cut down when people began to visit it to pray, so the place wouldn't become a shrine. Either way, the tree is gone. What lasts is the verse, which names them as people with whom Allah was pleased, remembered as the people of the tree. The pledge mattered not because the moment was safe, but because it wasn't.

segments.voice: Rest your right hand on your left, and think of a promise you made that matters: a vow at a wedding, a promise to a child, a promise to your faith or to yourself. Picture the moment you first made it. Then, quietly, make it again in the present tense, and if you pray, ask for help keeping it.

Your line: pledged under the tree. The tree is gone; the promise is what's remembered. See you tomorrow.

583.title: Lower your voices
583.hook: don't raise your voices above the Prophet's voice (49:2)
583.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to speak quietly in mosques, and visitors to the Prophet's mosque in Medina recall this verse at his grave; scholars also apply it to how hadith and his teaching are discussed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Bay'ah, the promise made hand in hand when the moment wasn't safe. Your line: pledged under the tree.

Two people talking over each other, then three, each a little louder, until nobody is listening and everyone is shouting a point at the ceiling. Usually it's an office or a family dinner. Once, the reports say, it happened in Medina, in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and the two rising voices belonged to Abu Bakr and 'Umar. That scene sits behind Surah Al-Hujurat, the Private Rooms, the forty-ninth surah: short, and something like a manual for how a community talks.

Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Lift not up your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor shout when speaking to him as ye shout one to another." Then a warning: lest your works be rendered vain while you don't notice. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari gives the occasion. A delegation came from the tribe of Banu Tamim, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar disagreed about who should be appointed over them. They argued in front of the Prophet until their voices rose. After this verse, the report says, 'Umar spoke to the Prophet so softly that he sometimes had to be asked to repeat himself. Another Companion took it even harder. Thabit ibn Qays had a naturally loud voice; he was the speaker for the Ansar. When the verse came down he stayed home, convinced his deeds were wasted. The Prophet noticed he was missing, sent someone to ask, and sent back a message: Thabit was not among the people of the fire, but of paradise. The next verse praises those who lower their voices in his presence. Commentators extend the courtesy beyond his lifetime: raising one's voice over his teaching is a related kind of disrespect. You may remember Luqman's advice to his son, earlier this year: walk modestly and lower your voice. Two surahs, two settings, the same instinct. Volume isn't the same as truth. Often it's a sign that listening has stopped.
screen: `LIFT NOT UP YOUR VOICES.` · `ABU BAKR AND 'UMAR, ARGUING.` · `THABIT, LOUD BY NATURE, STAYED HOME.` · `VOLUME ISN'T TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Picture the next room you'll be in with other people: a dinner table, a meeting, a group chat with a voice of its own. Choose one moment there to lower your volume on purpose, especially if you disagree, and let your breath be slow and low now so your body remembers it. If you pray, you can ask for a humble voice.
Abu Bakr. His voice, raised with 'Umar's in front of the Prophet, became the reason this verse came down, and he learned to speak so softly he had to repeat himself. Today's word.
Your line: the humble voice. A lower voice leaves room for listening. That's day five hundred eighty-three.

584.title: Verify the news
584.hook: if a wrongdoer brings news, verify it, lest you harm people unknowingly (49:6)
584.howItsDone: Islamic scholarship built whole sciences on checking reports, above all the study of hadith chains and narrators; Muslim teachers today cite 49:6 when urging people to check news before sharing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Abu Bakr, whose raised voice stands behind a verse on how to speak. Your line: the humble voice.

A screenshot arrives in the family group chat: something outrageous someone supposedly said. Within ten minutes it's been forwarded to three other groups, two aunts are furious, and nobody has asked the obvious question: is it real? The forward button is new. The problem isn't. In Medina, the commentators say, one unchecked account nearly sent armed men against a whole tribe. The verse tied to that story is a short rule about news.

Verse six, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." Evil-liver is Pickthall's word for fasiq, someone known to cross the line, whose word can't simply be trusted. Tidings is naba': news that carries weight, news people act on. And the command is one Arabic word: fatabayyanu. Make it clear. Find out. Here is the story commentators most often link to the verse. The Prophet ﷺ sent a man named al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to collect the zakat from the tribe of Banu al-Mustaliq. He turned back before reaching them and reported that they had refused to pay and meant to kill him. Anger rose in Medina, and in the version in Musnad Ahmad a party set out toward the tribe. On the way it met the tribe's chief, al-Harith ibn Dirar, coming the other way, puzzled that no collector had arrived. They had gathered the zakat and were waiting. The report was false. Commentators differ on the details, and some question parts of the account, but the shape is what the verse addresses. Notice the reason given: not just that lying is wrong, but that you'll harm people in ignorance and then be sorry. The responsibility sits with the listener, not only the speaker. In one of the recognized readings of the Qur'an, the same word is recited fatathabbatu: make sure, stand firm before acting. Two readings, one instruction: slow down before you strike.
screen: `FATABAYYANU: MAKE IT CLEAR.` · `NABA': NEWS PEOPLE ACT ON.` · `A FALSE REPORT ABOUT A WHOLE TRIBE.` · `THE LISTENER IS RESPONSIBLE TOO.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last week: was there something you passed on, out loud or with a forward, that you never checked? Don't scold yourself; just notice it, and hold one question ready for next time: who said this, and how do they know? If you pray, you can ask for a careful tongue.
Fatabayyanu: make it clear before you act, lest you harm people in ignorance, from 49:6. Today's word.
Your line: verify first. News is only as sound as its source. Day five hundred eighty-four, done.

585.title: Make peace between them
585.hook: believers are brothers, so make peace between your brothers (49:9–10)
585.carry: repair with fairness, so the thing can hold
585.howItsDone: In Muslim communities, elders, imams and family members act as go-betweens to reconcile quarrels, often citing 49:10 and the hadith that setting things right between people outranks voluntary worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fatabayyanu: make it clear before you act on news. Your line: verify first.

Some families have two people who don't speak. Two brothers after an inheritance. Two sisters after a wedding. Two old friends after one sentence nobody can take back. Everyone around them learns the choreography: separate invitations, careful seating, nobody saying the other's name. Years can go by like that, and it's easy to decide it isn't your business. Surah Al-Hujurat says otherwise. It makes the people standing around the quarrel responsible for ending it.

Verse nine begins with the hardest case: two groups of believers actually fighting. Make peace between them, it says; if one keeps transgressing, stand against it until it returns, then make peace with justice, and be fair. Then verse ten, in Pickthall's translation: "The believers are naught else than brothers. Therefor make peace between your brethren and observe your duty to Allah that haply ye may obtain mercy." Brothers here is ikhwah, and some commentators note it's the plural used for brothers by birth: the family word. The command, aslihu, comes from the root s-l-h, to set right, to repair. Islah is mending, the way you'd mend a torn thing so it can be used again. Peace here isn't passive. It's work, and it's assigned to bystanders. A hadith in the collections of Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi makes the point sharply. The Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions: shall I tell you of something better in rank than voluntary fasting, prayer and charity? They said yes. He said: setting things right between people, because ruining relations between people is the shaver, the thing that shaves away faith. Another hadith, in Bukhari, says that the one who makes peace between people, passing on good or saying good, is not a liar. The tradition gives the peacemaker room. And verse nine insists on justice: making peace isn't pretending nobody was wronged.
screen: `MAKE PEACE, WITH JUSTICE.` · `IKHWAH: THE FAMILY WORD.` · `ISLAH: MENDING A TORN THING.` · `BETTER THAN EXTRA FASTING AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people you know who are at odds: not a war you can't touch, but something close enough to reach. Picture each face, and think of one true, kind thing each has said or could say about the other; that's the material a peacemaker works with. If you pray, you can pray for them both.
Islah: mending, setting right, assigned by 49:10 to the people standing around a quarrel. Today's word.
Your line: repair with fairness, so the thing can hold. Peace like that takes work. See you tomorrow.

586.title: No mocking, no nicknames
586.hook: don't mock others, they may be better than you, and don't insult with names (49:11)
586.howItsDone: Muslim scholars count mocking and hurtful nicknames among the sins of the tongue; affectionate names a person welcomes, like Abu Hurayrah, are accepted, while names someone dislikes are avoided.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Islah, the mending the verse gives to bystanders. Your line: repair with fairness, so the thing can hold.
screen: `REPAIR WITH FAIRNESS, SO THE THING CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: Maybe you had one: the nickname from middle school that started as a joke about your ears, your name, your accent, your weight, and followed you for years. Some people laugh about theirs now. Some still flinch when they hear it. The people who gave them out mostly forgot within a week. Surah Al-Hujurat spends a whole verse on this, and the reason it gives is not the one you'd expect.

Verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they (are), nor let women (deride) women who may be better than they are; neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." Three things are named. Mocking, sakhar: laughing at someone to make them small. Defaming, lamz: the little dig, the jab disguised as a joke. And insulting with nicknames, tanabuz bil-alqab: the label that sticks. Then the reason. Not that mocking is rude, but that the one you mock may be better than you. You can see a person's ears or accent. You can't see their standing with God. Mockery assumes a ranking the mocker has no access to. A report in Sunan Abi Dawud gives the setting. A man from the Banu Salamah said the verse came down about them. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina, many men had two or three names, and when he called someone by one of them, people would say: Messenger of God, that one makes him angry. So the verse was revealed. Notice: the Prophet himself didn't know which names stung. Nicknames aren't always cruel. Many Companions carried names they loved, like Abu Hurayrah, father of the little cat. The line the scholars draw is the verse's own: whether the name is one the person dislikes. A hadith in Sahih Muslim sums it up: it is evil enough for a person to look down on his brother.
screen: `MOCKING, DIGS, AND LABELS THAT STICK.` · `THEY MAY BE BETTER THAN YOU.` · `NAMES THAT MADE SOMEONE ANGRY.` · `ABU HURAYRAH LOVED HIS.`

segments.voice: Think of the names you use for people, out loud or in your head: a coworker, a sibling, a politician, a driver who cut you off, and find one that's really a small insult. Picture that person hearing it, and set it down in favor of their real name. If you were given a name that still stings, you can let yourself set that down too, and if you pray, you can pray for them.
No mocking. The rule of 49:11: no deriding, no digs, no hurtful nicknames, because the one you mock may be better than you. Today's word.
Your line: they may be better. Nobody sees the whole of anyone else. That's day five hundred eighty-six.

587.title: Suspicion, spying, backbiting
587.hook: avoid much suspicion, don't spy, don't backbite, like eating your dead brother's flesh (49:12)
587.howItsDone: Muslim scholars count ghibah among the major sins of the tongue; they teach that when you hear backbiting you should defend the absent person or leave, and that someone you've backbitten should be prayed for or asked for forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no mocking, no nicknames, because the one you mock may be better. Your line: they may be better.

Someone leaves the room, and the conversation shifts half a degree. Did you notice how she…? Has he always been like that? Nobody's lying. Everything said is true, or true enough. And it can feel pleasant, that warm feeling of being inside a group that's outside someone else. Surah Al-Hujurat's twelfth verse answers that warm feeling with a hard, physical picture.
screen: `A HARD PICTURE FOR A WARM FEELING.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve moves in three steps, each closer to the mouth. Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime. And spy not, neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that." First, suspicion in the mind: zann, assuming the worst. Not all suspicion, but much of it, because some is sin. Second, spying, tajassus: going looking for what's hidden, checking someone's phone, digging for faults. Third, ghibah, backbiting: saying it. Then the image: a dead brother who can't defend himself, and you eating him. Commentators explain that the absent person is like the dead, present in the conversation, unable to answer. The verse doesn't explain the image. It asks: would you love that? And answers for you: you'd hate it. A hadith in Sahih Muslim defines ghibah exactly. The Prophet ﷺ asked: do you know what backbiting is? They said Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: mentioning your brother with something he would dislike. Someone asked: what if what I say is true? He said: if it's true, you have backbitten him. If it's false, you have slandered him. That's the surprise: ghibah is about the true things. Scholars do list exceptions, like seeking help against an injustice, or warning someone about a business partner or a marriage proposal, where the truth protects someone. But the default is clear, and the image leaves a simple test: would you say it with them in the room?
screen: `ZANN: ASSUMING THE WORST.` · `TAJASSUS: GOING LOOKING.` · `GHIBAH: SAYING IT.` · `TRUE, AND STILL BACKBITING.`

segments.voice: Picture the people you'll talk to today, and the people you're likely to talk about. For each absent person, imagine them sitting in the room, listening, and notice what you'd still say. If you pray, you can ask forgiveness for anyone you've spoken about.
Ghibah. Backbiting: mentioning someone in their absence with something they'd dislike, even when it's true, pictured in 49:12 as eating a dead brother's flesh. Today's word.
Your line: not behind their back. Sometimes silence is the kindest thing to offer. Until tomorrow.

588.title: To know one another
588.hook: We made you nations and tribes to know one another, and the most honored is the most mindful (49:13)
588.carry: made different to know each other
588.howItsDone: Muslims cite 49:13 against racism and tribalism, and the farewell sermon's words on Arab and non-Arab, red and black, are read in Friday sermons and at the pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ghibah, backbiting, even when what's said is true. Your line: not behind their back.

Arabic, Urdu, Malay, Turkish, Swahili, Hausa, Bosnian, French, English with a Texas accent. During the pilgrimage, all of it rises from one courtyard in Mecca, from faces of every shade in the same white cloth. The Qur'an has a verse about why humanity comes in so many kinds. It's in Surah Al-Hujurat, and for once in this surah it isn't addressed to believers. It's addressed to everyone.

Again and again, this surah has called: O ye who believe. Verse thirteen opens wider. Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Three moves. One origin: male and female, which commentators read as Adam and Hawwa, one family. Deliberate difference: nations and tribes, made on purpose. And the purpose, in one Arabic word: li-ta'arafu, so that you may know one another. The verb's form means mutual knowing, each side learning the other. Its root is shared with ma'ruf, the known good, and 'urf, custom. Difference here isn't a problem to solve. It's an introduction. Then the ranking is taken away from everything you can see. The noblest is the most mindful; the Arabic is atqakum, from taqwa, awareness of God. Not the richest, not the oldest family, not the right tribe. And taqwa can't be seen from outside; the verse leaves that judgment to the sight of Allah. A sermon attributed to the Prophet ﷺ during his farewell pilgrimage, recorded in the Musnad of Ahmad, put it plainly: no Arab has merit over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor red over black, nor black over red, except by taqwa. This week was the surah's lesson in talking well: a pledge, a lower voice, checked news, peace made, mocking dropped, backbiting refused. It ends with why the people across the table are different in the first place.
screen: `O MANKIND: THE VERSE OPENS WIDER.` · `ONE ORIGIN, DELIBERATE DIFFERENCE.` · `LI-TA'ARAFU: KNOWING EACH OTHER.` · `THE NOBLEST: THE MOST MINDFUL.`

segments.voice: Picture someone you see often whose background differs from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who runs the shop on the corner. Think about what you actually know of where they come from, maybe not much, and choose one kind question you'd like to ask them: a food, a holiday, a word in their language. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the variety of people.
Taqwa: the awareness of God, the only thing by which 49:13 says anyone is more noble than another. Today's word.
Your line: made different to know each other. Day five hundred eighty-eight, and a week complete.
